introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com et texte fantôme du verso (transparence du papier) ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 2 : faits cités de mémoire historique (Fourah Bay College 1827, Crowther évêque en 1864, Merrick à Bimbia en 1843, Saker à Douala dans les années 1840 et fondation de Victoria en 1858, Hope Waddell Institute 1895) ; la nuance sur l'effet réel des conversions reste une appréciation, non un chiffre.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Christian missionary successes in West Africa were largely religious. Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Christian missionary societies (the Church Missionary Society, the Methodists, the Baptists, the Basel Mission, the Catholic orders and others) arrived in West Africa in large numbers from the early nineteenth century. Their stated aim was to convert Africans. The question asks whether their achievements were mainly in the religious field. My view is that I only partly agree: religious success was real but limited, and the missionaries' more lasting achievements were educational, medical, linguistic, economic and political.

**1. Religious successes (the case for the statement).**
- Churches, mission stations and congregations were founded along the coast, in Sierra Leone, the Gold Coast, Nigeria and on the Cameroon coast (Joseph Merrick at Bimbia from 1843 and Alfred Saker at Douala and later Victoria from the 1840s and 1850s).
- African clergy emerged. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a freed slave, was consecrated first African Anglican bishop in 1864.
- The Bible was translated into African languages, and African churches later grew out of mission churches (the "Ethiopian" and independent churches).
- But conversions were slow in many areas. In the Muslim north and in areas with strong traditional religions, the missionaries won few converts, and many converts mixed old and new beliefs.

**2. Educational successes.**
- Missionaries opened primary schools and later secondary schools and colleges. Fourah Bay College (founded 1827 in Freetown) trained teachers and clergy and became a university college. Others included the Methodist and Presbyterian schools of the Gold Coast and the Hope Waddell Training Institute at Calabar (1895).
- Literacy in African languages (Yoruba, Twi, Efik, Duala and others) grew, hymns and grammars were printed, and educated Africans became clerks, teachers, lawyers and, later, nationalist leaders.

**3. Medical and social successes.**
- Mission hospitals and dispensaries treated disease and fought leprosy; the use of quinine reduced the death rate among Europeans and made travel inland possible.
- Missionaries campaigned against practices they judged harmful, such as the killing of twins in Calabar (Mary Slessor) and human sacrifice, and helped freed slaves.

**4. Economic successes.**
- They encouraged "legitimate commerce" in place of the slave trade: new crops, handicrafts and carpentry, building skills and printing. Their stations taught new methods of farming.
- Some missions ran trading businesses or supported traders, linking Africans to world markets.

**5. Political successes (and their cost).**
- Missionaries acted as advisers and interpreters, drew up treaties and prepared the way for colonial rule. In Abeokuta (Henry Townsend), at Calabar and on the Cameroon coast, they were often the first Europeans to deal with local rulers, and their appeals brought consuls and then colonial governments.
- Some missionaries defended Africans against abuses; others undermined African culture and authority, so their influence was not always welcome.

**Evaluation and conclusion.** The statement is only partly true. The religious success was real, but in numbers and in lasting effect it was smaller than the success in education, health, language and economic change, which created the western-educated class that led the independence movements. The missionaries' political role, though often unintended, was also important. I therefore do not fully agree: missionary successes were broad, and religion was only one of several fields in which they succeeded.
